title: Can you have two main methods in a Java application?
shortTitle: Can you have two main methods in a Java application?
keyPoints: Yes – multiple classes in the same project can each have their own main(String[] args)
You choose which one to run: java com.bank.TransferApp or java com.bank.ReportApp
In a jar, the Main-Class attribute in MANIFEST.MF specifies the default entry point
Within a single class, you can also overload main (different parameter types), but only String[] is the entry point
This is common in banking: one main for the batch service, one for the API server, one for migration tools

s1_definition.oneliner: Yes. Multiple classes can each have main(String[] args). You choose which one to run by specifying the class name. In a jar, the MANIFEST.MF Main-Class attribute selects the default.
s1_definition.profdef:
Two separate meanings of "two main methods":

- **Multiple classes with main:** Perfectly legal and common. Each class is an independent entry point. You choose which to run via `java ClassName` or the jar manifest.
- **Overloaded main in one class:** Also legal. `main(String[])` and `main(int)` can coexist. Only the `String[]` version is the JVM entry point.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank building with multiple front doors – one for retail customers, one for corporate, one for staff. Each door (main method in a different class) leads to a different service. The signage on the building (MANIFEST.MF) indicates which door is the default entrance.

sections.s2_detail:
### Multiple classes with main

```java
// File: TransferApp.java
package com.bank;
public class TransferApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Running transfer batch...");
    }
}

// File: ReportApp.java
package com.bank;
public class ReportApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Running daily report...");
    }
}
```

```bash
# Choose which to run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.TransferApp
# Output: Running transfer batch...

java -cp target/classes com.bank.ReportApp
# Output: Running daily report...
```

### How does the jar manifest work?

```text
# META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
Main-Class: com.bank.TransferApp
```

```bash
# Default entry point from manifest
java -jar bank-service.jar
# Runs com.bank.TransferApp.main()

# Override with explicit class
java -cp bank-service.jar com.bank.ReportApp
# Runs com.bank.ReportApp.main()
```

### When is this useful in banking?

| Class | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `TransferBatchApp` | Nightly batch transfer processing |
| `InterestCalculationApp` | Monthly interest computation |
| `MigrationApp` | One-time data migration tool |
| `ApiServerApp` | Spring Boot REST API server |

Each is a separate entry point in the same codebase, sharing the same domain classes.

### What about Maven/Gradle configuration?

```xml
<!-- Maven: specify main class in pom.xml -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <archive>
            <manifest>
                <mainClass>com.bank.TransferBatchApp</mainClass>
            </manifest>
        </archive>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

### What are common mistakes?

- **Forgetting to set Main-Class in the manifest.** `java -jar app.jar` fails with "no main manifest attribute."
- **Two main methods in the same class with same parameters.** That is a compile error (duplicate method), not overloading.
- **Assuming the JVM picks one automatically.** You must specify which class to run.

### What should a senior engineer know?

- **Spring Boot apps have one @SpringBootApplication main.** Additional entry points should be separate classes or use Spring profiles.
- **Docker ENTRYPOINT specifies the main class.** `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]` uses the manifest. Override with `ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-cp", "app.jar", "com.bank.MigrationApp"]`.
- **Gradle `application` plugin** uses `mainClass.set('com.bank.TransferApp')` to configure the default entry point.
sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Project with multiple main classes:

  com.bank.TransferBatchApp.main(String[])
  com.bank.ReportApp.main(String[])
  com.bank.MigrationApp.main(String[])
    │
    ├─ java -jar app.jar          → uses MANIFEST.MF Main-Class
    ├─ java -cp app.jar com.bank.ReportApp  → explicit class
    └─ Docker ENTRYPOINT          → specifies which to run
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, you can have multiple main methods in a Java application. Each class can have its own `public static void main(String[] args)`, and you choose which one to run by specifying the class name. In a jar file, the MANIFEST.MF Main-Class attribute selects the default entry point.

This is common in banking projects: one main for the batch processor, one for the API server, one for migration tools, all sharing the same domain classes and data access layer.

One sentence to remember: multiple classes can each have main – you choose which one to run via the command line or the jar manifest.
